item.title: Towards unsupervised representation learning for quantum data: quantum models with inference and generation
item.description:
Pay dirt theory — Unsupervised representation learning on quantum data requires non-linear data extension maps; joint visible-latent models admitting both inference and generation factorisations exist under the Leifer-Spekkens state-over-time map and are exactly the bipartite states with positive partial transpose (PPT).

Grade 0.459 · 3.1σ above the day's baseline · matched “Quantum machine learning” · Robin Lorenz, Eric Brunner, Marcello Benedetti

Figure

Venn diagram showing the nested hierarchy of ambiguous state sets CX-PPT, PPT, and DX-PPT within the space of all bipartite states S(𝒳⊗𝒴).

Asks

How can unsupervised representation learning with compatible inference and generation channels be formulated for coherent quantum data lacking a classical probability chain rule?

But

Restricted to finite-dimensional bipartite systems; excludes non-PPT entangled states from exact Leifer-Spekkens inference and generation.

Tools

state-over-time (SOT) maps · Leifer-Spekkens formalism · PPT entanglement criterion · Jamiołkowski isomorphism · Lyapunov equations

Abstract

With quantum sensors, simulators and networks emerging, a future of quantum technology may produce quantum states as data---that is, coherently rather than as classical measurement records---thus motivating the study of suitable quantum generalisations of modern machine learning, including the automated, unsupervised extraction of useful representations. Two ingredients are central to the latter: inference, mapping observations to latent representations, and generation, mapping latent states back to synthetic data. Both are related to each other and to joint distributions for training models by the chain-rule of classical probability theory. The fact that quantum states however lack such universal, standard factorisation property thus poses a challenge. Here we develop a conceptual and mathematical framework for unsupervised representation learning from quantum data. Models are joint quantum states over visible and latent systems; state-over-time maps provide a notion of factorisation into a marginal state and inference (generation) channel; models with inference (generation) are ambiguous states---states for which such factorisation obtains---subject to a further consistency condition on extended inference maps as data extension. These stipulations are restrictive: we show that non-trivial models must feature non-linear such maps to the extended space. For three representative state-over-time maps, we completely characterise the ambiguous states, uncovering a hierarchy tied to the positive-partial-transpose (PPT) criterion from entanglement theory. Notably, the Leifer-Spekkens construction supports inference and generation exactly for model classes of PPT states, thus allowing genuinely quantum visible-latent correlations. We also formulate quantum counterparts of exact and approximate inference training, explore weaker notions of data extension and sketch a future research programme.

item.title: Verifiable quantum advantage in extremely low depth
item.description:
Pay dirt new result — Constructed classically verifiable quantum advantage sampling problem runnable on 𝖰𝖭𝖢0[log⁡log⁡] circuits (one- and two-qubit gates) or 𝖰𝖠𝖢0 circuits (constant depth with unbounded fan-in gates), requiring no mid-circuit measurements or feed-forward.

Grade 0.398 · 2.2σ above the day's baseline · matched “Power of data in quantum machine learning” · Alexandru Gheorghiu

Asks

Can classically verifiable quantum advantage be achieved with shallow quantum circuits without requiring mid-circuit measurements or adaptive feed-forward?

Before

Arabadjieva et al. (2025) achieved single-round LWE-based proofs of quantumness, but required deeper circuits.

But

Relies on lattice knowledge assumption and a strengthened variant of the adaptive-hardcore-bit property of LWE; classical hardness is computational.

Tools

Learning with Errors (LWE) · QNC⁰[loglog] circuits · QAC⁰ circuits · lattice knowledge assumptions · strengthened adaptive-hardcore-bit property

Abstract

We give a sampling problem that is solvable by shallow quantum circuits, hard for polynomial-time classical algorithms under lattice-based assumptions, and efficiently verifiable by a classical computer. The quantum sampler admits two implementations: one uses log-logarithmic-depth quantum circuits with one- and two-qubit gates, i.e., QNC⁰[loglog] circuits, while the other uses constant-depth quantum circuits with unbounded fan-in gates, i.e., QAC⁰ circuits. Our construction can be seen as compiling the Learning with Errors (LWE)-based single-round proof of quantumness of Arabadjieva et al. (2025) to very low depth. The price paid for this compilation is the reliance on less standard, though well-motivated, assumptions: in addition to the lattice knowledge assumption used by Arabadjieva et al. (2025), we require a strengthened variant of the adaptive-hardcore-bit property of LWE, for which we provide supporting evidence. Unlike previous low-depth proofs of quantumness, the quantum computation here requires no mid-circuit measurements or feed-forward: it consists only of running a shallow circuit and sampling from its output distribution. This shows that shallow quantum circuits have sufficient structure to solve certain classically hard tasks whose solutions can be verified efficiently.

item.title: A Dynamic Intermediate Representation for Hybrid Quantum-Classical Programs
item.description:
Worth a look new method — Dynamic intermediate representation (IR) elevates quantum gates to first-class values for dynamic creation, composition, and control steered by classical runtime computation.

Grade 0.361 · 1.7σ above the day's baseline · matched “Power of data in quantum machine learning” · Alex Rice, Chris Heunen, Tobias Grosser

Asks

How to represent hybrid quantum-classical programs where gate choices depend on runtime data, classical control, or measurement results within a unified intermediate representation?

Before

Static circuit-model intermediate representations restricted to fixed sequences of gates without native support for dynamic runtime gate construction or classical-quantum steering.

Tools

dynamic intermediate representation (IR) · first-class gate value model · compiler analysis and transformation suite

Abstract

Quantum compilers typically follow the circuit model, representing programs as fixed sequences of gates. This static view breaks down in hybrid quantum-classical applications, where gate choices depend on runtime data or measurement results. We introduce a new Intermediate Representation (IR) that elevates gates to first-class values, enabling their dynamic creation, composition, and control. This unified representation allows classical computation to steer quantum behaviour, capturing phenomena including stochastic gate selection, adaptive error correction, and measurement-driven computation within a single framework. Case studies in noise modelling, randomised compilation, error correction, and measurement-based quantum computing show that our IR expresses these programs compactly and supports optimisations that were not possible in the circuit model. Evaluation on a benchmark suite of hybrid quantum-classical programs indicates that our IR represents programs compactly and facilitates compiler analysis and transformation.

item.title: Exact Virtual Channel Programming with Vanishing Excess Overhead
item.description:
Worth a look theory — Exact reconstruction of d-dimensional channel output observables using physical channels and classical post-processing requires quasiprobability sampling overhead ν1(CPTPd⁡)=2d2−3+2/d2 for one Choi program copy, and obeys νk(CPTPd⁡)=1+(d2−1)/(2k)+o(k−1) for k copies.

Grade 0.355 · 1.6σ above the day's baseline · matched “Power of data in quantum machine learning” · Mingrui Jing, Mengbo Guo, Hongshun Yao, Xin Wang

Figure

Schematic comparing exact physical channel programming, which is obstructed for continuous families by finite memory, with exact virtual programming using normalized Choi states and norm-optimal quasi-decomposition sampling.

Asks

Can multiple copies of a physical program state reduce the sampling cost of exact output-observable reconstruction for arbitrary quantum channels?

But

Product normalized Choi state programs πℰ⊗k; fixed dimension d with k→∞; shot overhead excludes program preparation, memory lifetime, retriever complexity, and fault tolerance.

Tools

deterministic port-based teleportation · quasiprobability channel decomposition · semidefinite programming with walled Brauer symmetry · local quantum estimation / Cramér-Rao bounds

Abstract

A finite-dimensional physical processor cannot exactly program a continuous family of distinct unitary channels. We show that this obstruction becomes quantitative when the target channel is stored in a normalized Choi state and its output observables are reconstructed by sampling physical channels and classically post-processing their measurement outcomes. For arbitrary d-dimensional channels, we construct a target-independent exact reconstruction protocol and prove the optimal one-copy sampling overhead, which grows quadratically with system dimension. We further prove the sharp fixed-d law that the excess overhead vanishes inversely with the number of identical Choi programs. The upper bound combines deterministic port-based teleportation with a quasi-decomposition that corrects its depolarizing distortion. The converse maps any low-overhead reconstruction protocol to a physical learner of unknown unitaries and uses local quantum estimation to recover the same leading coefficient. These results recast the universal no-programming obstruction as a quantitative trade-off between quantum program memory and classical sampling, with a leading cost that reflects the locally learnable unitary degrees of freedom.
